title: Importance of cultural context in AI understanding | Cohere
gist: A Cohere Labs open-science project, started by Hungarian diplomat Boczka Karoly's culture-specific riddles, grew to 100+ contributors from 50+ countries and found that English-heavy models sound fluent but lack cultural knowledge, hallucinate, and almost never say 'I don't know'. Participants report near-zero knowledge of Buginese and warn that authoritative-sounding wrong answers are the main risk.

insights.claim: Cohere Labs' cultural riddle project began when Hungarian diplomat Boczka Károly built Hungarian trivia-style riddles to test whether AI models recognize cultural clues, and found their answers sounded right but were wrong.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Grassroots, culture-specific tests can expose gaps that standard English benchmarks miss.
insights.locator: Hungarian diplomat Boczka Károly was actively exploring

insights.claim: Models tested on the Hungarian riddles were missing culturally specific facts and in certain instances hallucinated, showing a gap between AI fluency and cultural knowledge.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Fluency is a poor proxy for competence in non-English, culturally grounded tasks; relevant for global enterprise deployment.
insights.quote: The models’ answers sounded right, but they weren't right.
insights.locator: Hungarian diplomat Boczka Károly was actively exploring

insights.claim: Julia Kreutzer, Staff Research Scientist at Cohere Labs, joined Boczka to scale the project globally to test fluency, logic and reasoning in models trained mostly on English data and the blind spots behind each answer.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Cohere Labs is positioning itself around multilingual and cultural evaluation of models.
insights.locator: In an open-science community discussion around culture in AI

insights.claim: The riddle project required no expertise beyond identification with a culture and a commitment to writing and evaluating riddles, with an open call on social media and within Cohere Labs communities and no entry criteria.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Crowdsourcing cultural knowledge with low barriers is a cheap route to multilingual evaluation data.
insights.locator: Participation in the project did not require expertise

insights.claim: The community organized on Discord and built its own benchmarks across cultural segments such as sports, history and politics, with each question designed as a riddle.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Community-built benchmarks are an emerging source of evaluation data outside big labs.

insights.claim: The project grew to more than 100 contributors from more than 50 countries.
insights.speaker: Boczka Károly
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of volunteer participation Cohere Labs can mobilize for open research.
insights.quote: We had more than 100 contributors from more than 50 countries.
insights.locator: Mr. Boczka's idea quickly grew into an international initiative

insights.claim: Participant Henry Gagnier, a 16-year-old American, argues that real cultural knowledge rather than AI skills is what helps build this kind of benchmark, so AI research needs people from many cultures.
insights.speaker: Henry Gagnier
insights.so_what: Cultural-evaluation data depends on diverse human contributors, not only on engineers.
insights.locator: While most teenagers might be hesitant

insights.claim: Gagnier found the tested models had virtually zero knowledge of Buginese, a fairly frequently spoken language, which translated into zero knowledge of the culture under the team's evaluation.
insights.speaker: Henry Gagnier
insights.so_what: Even moderately widespread languages can be unsupported, a market opening for models with stronger multilingual coverage.
insights.quote: These models don't know this language at all
insights.locator: AI’s struggle with cultural riddles across different languages

insights.claim: The article argues that AI's struggle with cultural riddles across languages and contexts is potentially one of the most significant challenges in developing models.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Cultural and linguistic coverage may become a differentiator for model vendors targeting global enterprise customers.
insights.locator: AI’s struggle with cultural riddles across different languages

insights.claim: Retired teacher Jane Smith observed that the models rarely answered 'I don't know' and instead gave authoritative-sounding answers that would lead one to think the model knows what it is talking about.
insights.speaker: Jane Smith
insights.so_what: Poor calibration of uncertainty is a deployment risk; evaluate abstention behavior, not just accuracy.
insights.locator: Mrs. Smith reveals a widely shared societal concern

insights.claim: Smith says the scary part is that wrong model answers sound authoritative while people are looking for authoritative answers, so confident-sounding errors are more dangerous than obvious ones.
insights.speaker: Jane Smith
insights.so_what: User demand for authority plus model overconfidence compounds misinformation risk in enterprise and consumer use.
insights.quote: The scary part to me is that it sounds so authoritative and people are looking for authoritative answers.

insights.claim: Smith argues that the danger is not AI itself but humanity's lack of critical thinking, summed up as 'To err is AI. To critically think is human.'
insights.speaker: Jane Smith
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop verification remains the control against confident model errors.
insights.quote: To err is AI. To critically think is human.
insights.locator: In an age where some worry

insights.claim: Cohere Labs is working on better contextual understanding by studying confidence in today's models.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Confidence calibration is an active research direction at Cohere; watch for resulting product features.
insights.locator: There is an interesting space between human cognition

insights.claim: Jane Smith applied a teacher's approach of working backwards from a wrong answer to find what led to it, and used animals like tigers or crabs in riddles to gamify the logic.
insights.speaker: Jane Smith
insights.so_what: Error-tracing methods from education can inform model failure analysis.

insights.claim: Each solved riddle or generated puzzle became a data point that refined the project's understanding of language and logic.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Riddles provide an interpretation-focused evaluation format that complements factual QA benchmarks.
